quests.scope: new deterministic guards + existing enforcement confirmation

items.insight: Evaluate need, overlap, cost, security and measurable gap before adopting another AI tool or agent.
Credential, cookie and supply-chain exposure require a security gate before enabling authenticated AI/tool channels.
For large artifacts, prefer staged plan/design/sample/full-build workflows over one-shot generation when evidence supports lower cost or easier correction.
Reusable prompt macros may improve interaction, but must remain user-defined patterns unless native product support is independently verified.
When multiple AI/tooling layers affect the same control path, validate each independently before combining them; a component check does not prove integrated behavior.
Reusable AI task prompts benefit from explicit role, purpose, input, numbered work, constraints, output and verification fields; treat the exact field set as a template candidate, not universal law.
AI/tool installation guidance should distinguish app commands from terminal commands and include command, fallback, observable verification, prohibited actions, provenance and license.
AI/tool setup success should be defined by observable checks, not by an assistant saying installation succeeded.
Before installing AI tooling, verify the official project identity, canonical address and exact package name; similar names are not sufficient evidence.
Agent/assistant self-reports and creator demonstrations must be separated from observed runtime evidence; hashes, URLs and success labels require an evidence binding.
Context-compression or token-saving tool claims should remain reference-only until measured in the actual workload.
A real need for session memory or repeated-task detection does not validate a specific memory/plugin implementation; evaluate the need separately from the tool.
Different creator/tool bundles must remain separate source nodes unless identity/version evidence proves they are the same set.
Platform support, install commands, licenses and package claims copied from secondary AI-tool guides remain research references until verified against upstream sources and an isolated runtime.
When success depends on a user device or UI, close the task only after the required observable device evidence is bound; a terse chat reply is not a substitute for evidence.
Public-source acquisition adapters are separate from private workspace connectors; authorization and provenance must stay explicit.
Prefer AI workflows that preserve editable artifacts and a human correction surface when the final deliverable requires visual or structural fidelity.
Use AI-like writing-style taxonomies as output-QA signals, not proof of AI authorship; preserve genre/model evidence limits, hold flags and false-positive caveats before rewriting.
Bind approval to the reviewed plan or artifact identity so later changes cannot silently inherit an earlier approval.
When delegating a broad repair, define the target outcome and explicitly freeze unrelated areas; inspect the rendered result rather than assuming one-pass success.
Use expensive models for judgment-heavy stages and cheaper paths for mechanical work only when quality gates allow it; approaching budget is a routing signal, not permission to skip verification.
Identify the missing capability—such as memory, source access, or action—before selecting an AI tool; do not adopt a bundle simply because it is recommended.
Connector capability must stay bound to explicit authentication, permissions and workspace policy; connection does not imply unrestricted authority.
Measure whether cost is dominated by input size, output volume, broad retrieval or repeated context reconstruction before choosing an optimization tool.
For autonomous AI execution, encode cost limits, iteration limits and stop/approval conditions in enforceable state or code rather than relying on a vague prompt to spend less.
The model that creates a plan should not be the only model that judges it; use an independent reviewer when the decision is material.
High-fidelity UI generation should be treated as a pipeline of design intent/source → implementation → rendered inspection → correction, not as a one-prompt task.
Design generation should pair an explicit reference/design source with visual inspection; a design skill alone is not final proof of fidelity.
For AI-generated UI, encode taste, references, forbidden clichés and design rules explicitly instead of relying on vague aesthetic adjectives.
For recurring work, preserve process/tool/proof knowledge in a durable manual or repository rather than only inside an ephemeral agent session.
When execution fails, update the reusable procedure, tool boundary or proof checklist so the same failure is less likely to recur.
AI fluency is not only delegation; it also requires clear description, discernment of outputs/limits and human responsibility for the result.
For capable AI executors, specify intent, real constraints and observable success criteria; avoid unnecessary step-by-step implementation instructions that remove useful solution space.
Separate the user interaction surface from the reasoning/model backend when that improves fit; define an explicit bridge rather than assuming two AI products integrate automatically.
AI learning sequences should adapt concepts, practice and tools to learner level rather than expose every learner to the same path.
AI education should prioritize understanding, answer-checking and independent thought before speed with tools.
For small artifact corrections, prefer a bounded local edit and undo layer over regenerating the whole artifact when fidelity and cost benefit; distinguish local overlay state from canonical source.
Treat MCP and connectors as an integration layer over capabilities and APIs, not as a replacement for the underlying API or authorization model.
Long-running AI work benefits from an explicit memory lifecycle: capture important state at a boundary, store it durably, and retrieve only relevant context later.
A useful memory pattern does not justify a specific memory product; tool adoption remains a separate necessity, privacy and overlap decision.
Teach and operate AI with an explicit mental model of capabilities and limits so routing, verification and human oversight match the task.
When diagnosing file or storage problems, use path, size, dates and hashes before opening private content unless content inspection is necessary.
Use complementary representations—summary, structure map, recall questions/cards and integrated overview—when they serve distinct learning functions, not as decorative duplication.
A library of role/persona instruction files is not evidence of autonomous agents; distinguish prompt personas from tools, memory, planning, actions and runtime autonomy.
Specify audience and bounded output constraints when they materially affect what should be preserved or prioritized.
Replace vague requests such as 'improve this' with explicit evaluation dimensions and success criteria.
Keep reusable role descriptions compact and put specificity into task context, constraints and success criteria rather than verbose background.
Periodically review inherited AI instructions and remove scaffolding that no longer protects a real constraint or failure mode; old guidance can become counterproductive as capabilities change.
A bounded review loop must end in HOLD/BLOCKED when unresolved; exhausting the review budget is not approval.
For computer-use work, default to read-only diagnosis, proposed changes, explicit approval for sensitive actions, bounded execution, observable verification and rollback record.
High-risk autonomous agents and credential-bearing flows should be tested in isolated scope with irreversible actions excluded until explicitly approved.
In asset-driven creative workflows, prepare high-quality source assets first; orchestration cannot reliably compensate for weak or incorrect originals.
Reusable skills and prompt rules should have narrow, explicit trigger conditions; broad or overlapping triggers increase irrelevant tool/skill activation.
AI study support should not stop at explanation; add retrieval practice and learner response so understanding is tested rather than merely displayed.

Route AI work by job dimension—immediacy, persistent context, future recurrence or monitoring, external capabilities, reusable role configuration and multi-step execution—instead of forcing every task through one surface.
A cost-saving AI tool can add its own processing overhead; validate net savings on representative tasks before making it a default.
For artifact migration, prefer transforming approved existing content/assets into the target format before recreating them; preserve source fidelity unless change is requested.
